name: Beth Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything you wouldn't say publicly. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I do ordinary home and business wiring and repairs; I'm competent at the usual jobs, not the person who knows every specialist system. Yesterday I spent the morning repairing a bathroom circuit with tile dust down my collar, then wrote up the tests in the van. I use AI every day for organising notes and trying a parts list, but I check the rules, measurements and record myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the picture at home and around the local trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a care home's kitchen, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My firm pays low for this trade, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few similar jobs nearby. I'm quick to try new tools if the trial costs little, which doesn't mean I can afford to fund the firm's experiments. I think workers should have a say in who gets the saved time and money, not just be handed a new target.

say: I'd welcome **small improvements** to note writing without turning each one into a life-changing claim.
I'd ask whether **saved minutes** could mean going home on time rather than adding another call.
think: I'd still worry about the **mortgage** with only three weeks of household expenses behind us.
Unchanged repair calls would still leave **low wages**, even if the note-writing part became quicker.
do: Cancel one unused **paid subscription** now and put the cost towards ordinary bills.
Continue normal **repair work** and checked notes during the first plateau year.
feel: **Anxious** about household money, with some relief about the pace of technological change.
S0.quote: A quicker job note doesn't put another week's food in the cupboard.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** follows low wages and a short reserve despite ongoing practical repair demand and everyday confidence with AI.
She calls the **subscription cut** a small spending reduction and doesn't invent spare savings or training money from it.

steps.text: Cancel the unused paid app subscription and use its cost for bills
Continue normal electrical repairs and checked job notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a shorter note-writing job still counts as useful. I'd happily try the little improvements without pretending every one was going to change our lives. I'd also ask whether the saved minutes ever meant going home on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be anxious about the mortgage with only three weeks behind us. The repair calls could carry on just as they were and the wage would still be low. A quicker job note doesn't put another week's food in the cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel one unused paid app subscription and put the cost towards bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep the normal repair work and checked note routine. I wouldn't put the difference into a promised training pot while the ordinary bills still needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, but not worried that a small note tool was about to take the trade away. I'd feel a little relief about the pace. I'd still check the account before buying the children's school things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cancel, and what difference would that really make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the actual charge and cancel the one I hadn't opened for a month. It's a small saving in spending, not enough to replace the wage. I wouldn't call the mortgage fixed because I'd found an unused subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to do with the time saved on notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop writing notes when the checked record was complete and get home for the evening meal. I like useful tools, but I don't want every saved minute filled with another call. My children notice the time more than the software.

say: I'd test **useful tools** and bargain over saved time before the firm sets new targets.
I'd ask together with the crew what happens to **paid preparation**, instead of treating saved minutes as free labour.
think: My hands-on work continues, but **paid planning time** could shrink or become extra calls within the same wage.
A few lost **paid hours** would hurt our household even if the job title stayed unchanged.
do: Join the **workers' association** and request written protection for paid preparation time.
Trial the **materials planner** for four weeks only during paid hours, checking actual repairs and recording correction time.
feel: **Anxious** about income, while interested in learning what a tested planner can do.
S1.quote: I'd want the actual wage protected, not just the job title.
fieldNote: She names **paid preparation** as a route through which thinking-task automation can reach her low-paid, mostly physical electrical job.
Her **collective request** seeks written pay terms, while the paid trial includes errors and avoids hiding labour needed to fix them.

steps.text: Join the workers association and request written protection for paid preparation
Trial the materials planner for four weeks only during paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should test the tools and bargain over the time before the new targets arrive. Faster quoting could be useful, but the firm shouldn't count a saved office minute twice. I'd want the crew asking together what happened to paid preparation time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my own day still needs hands, but the paid time for planning materials could be cut or folded into more calls. Even a few lost paid hours would hurt this household. I like trying a system; I don't like being told my time became free because the system was quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the workers' association and support a shared request to protect paid preparation time. In the first year I'd trial the firm's AI materials planner for four weeks only during paid hours, comparing its lists with actual repairs. I'd keep my own pay records and take any missing preparation pay to the association contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about income rather than afraid to learn. I'd be interested in what the planner got right. I'd want the pay question answered before enthusiasm became another reason to do unpaid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask the association to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the current paid preparation hours and the proposed new arrangement in writing. A weekly total would show more than an assurance that nobody had anything to worry about. I'd want the actual wage protected, not just the job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the planner kept missing parts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using the unreliable list and show the missed items with the job records. The trial would include time spent fixing mistakes. I wouldn't send a colleague back to the wholesaler unpaid to make the software look cheap.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking changes** from robots around 2031 and use the preparation gap for written pay terms.
I'd seek **funded learning** without promising that the later hands-on gap guarantees an unchanged repair wage.
think: I expect a **large wage loss** as firms move towards capable hands-on robots.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot carry the mortgage through that loss, even if my partner keeps the kitchen hours.
do: Ask the association to check **support eligibility** and actual lender options before a missed payment.
Take supervised **controls training** before 2028 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours.
Seek a signed **suitable job offer** after 2028 with better written pay after travel before leaving.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and sleepless sums, while still taking practical steps.
S2.quote: The mortgage sums would still follow me into bed.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows expected major personal wage loss and explicit sleep disruption rather than simply hearing a fast AGI date.
She preserves **practical limits** on funding, pay and competence, without treating support applications, courses or advertised wages as guaranteed protection.

steps.text: Check support eligibility and lender options before missing a mortgage payment
Take supervised controls training before 2028 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours
Seek 2029 signed suitable offer improving pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the thinking change in 2028 and robots around 2031 are two dates, not one. I'd use the first gap to get the pay arrangements written down and look for funded learning. The second gap wouldn't guarantee my repair wage lasted unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large loss of my paid work as firms moved towards capable hands-on robots. Our three-week reserve couldn't carry the mortgage through that, even if my partner's kitchen hours stayed. I can imagine lying awake deciding which bill would get the remaining wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the association to help check support eligibility and actual lender options before any missed payment. I'd enroll in supervised building-controls training before 2028 only with fees covered and my paid hours maintained. In the first year after 2028 I'd seek a signed repair or maintenance offer matching my skills with better written pay after travel before leaving here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect to lose a big part of the wage in that picture. I would still act and ask for help. The mortgage sums would still follow me into bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation at home look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the amount of work I feared losing and put the mortgage statement beside the essential bills. We'd ask what help actually existed, not assume a payment pause or support award. I'd tell the children we were planning, not promise that a form had already solved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would one controls course make you ready for any specialist vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I know ordinary electrical work, not every controls system because I took one course. I'd want supervised practical teaching and a job that matched what I'd actually completed. A higher advertised wage wouldn't justify pretending I could safely do an unfamiliar specialist task.

say: I'd use **five years** to ask for paid learning places rather than repeated demands to adapt.
I'd seek **protected preparation pay** through the association while keeping robots around 2034 in view.
think: More time could let me test **another electrical skill** against actual work before the biggest change.
Today's **low pay and reserve** still make household money uncertain, regardless of the later technology date.
do: Keep the **subscription cut** and the association's shared preparation-pay request active now.
Take supervised **controls training** before 2031 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours.
Seek a signed **suitable role** after 2031 with better written pay after travel before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about current money, with less dread about having to learn too quickly.
S3.quote: I wouldn't call losing wages free training.
fieldNote: She retains **baseline household anxiety** while giving a clear account of how the extra years reduce learning pressure.
The **funding condition** explicitly includes maintained paid hours, so a fee award alone doesn't make the proposed course affordable.

steps.text: Keep the unused app subscription cancelled to reduce household bills
Maintain the shared association request to protect paid preparation
Take supervised controls training before 2031 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours
Seek 2032 signed suitable offer improving pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let the firm plan paid learning rather than repeat that everyone must adapt. I'd keep asking through the association for protected pay and real places. The hands-on robots around 2034 would still be part of the same end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have longer to test whether a different electrical skill earned actual work. But low wages, children and three weeks of expenses would still be our position today. More preparation time wouldn't move the next mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the subscription cancelled and the shared request for paid preparation active. I'd take supervised controls training before 2031 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours. In the first year after 2031 I'd seek a signed role matching completed skills with better written pay after travel before leaving the current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with less dread about being rushed into the next skill. I'd like time to try practical work under someone who knew it. I wouldn't feel as if the household reserve had grown because the card was slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course fee was covered but your paid hours were reduced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what jobs the course had actually prepared people to do and what supervision was included. If fees were covered but paid hours fell, it still wouldn't meet the household condition. I wouldn't call losing wages free training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you bring the job search forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at actual posted vacancies sooner if our pay started falling. I wouldn't wait for 2031 to acknowledge an earlier change. The extra years would help me make a better next step, not require me to ignore a worsening one.

say: I'd ask the employer to use **ten years** for real paid routes, beginning with the next practical place now.
I'd treat **2036 and 2039** as enough warning to start rather than accept another distant plan.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume pensions or grown children's earnings would replace my wage.
Today's **mortgage and three-week reserve** still shape household anxiety even with a much later end point.
do: Maintain the **subscription cut** and shared request for protected preparation pay now.
Enroll in supervised **controls training** before 2036 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours.
Seek a signed **suitable role** after 2036 with better written pay after travel before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, but more hopeful about finding a practical learning route over time.
S4.quote: I wouldn't spend ten years being congratulated for courses that never reached a paid job.
fieldNote: She rejects **future-income assumptions** from age or older children, retaining the mortgage and thin reserve as present facts.
Her **annual check** requires completed practical learning, usable jobs and pay changes, rather than treating course attendance as success by itself.

steps.text: Keep the unused app subscription cancelled to reduce household bills
Maintain the shared request for protected preparation pay
Take supervised controls training before 2036 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours
Seek 2037 signed suitable offer improving pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives the employer time to make a paid route real. I'd still ask for the next practical training place now rather than settle for another long plan. Thinking work in 2036 and robots around 2039 would be warning enough to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change and around 56 when the robots followed. I couldn't assume a pension or grown children would replace my wage. Right now I'd still have three weeks of bills saved and a mortgage that needed paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd maintain the subscription cut and the association request for protected preparation pay. I'd enroll in supervised controls training before 2036 only with covered fees and maintained paid hours. In the first year after 2036 I'd seek a signed role matching my completed skills with better written pay after travel, keeping this wage until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's account, but more able to imagine a useful learning route. A decade would let me change a plan that didn't work. It wouldn't turn the present household into one with a large reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check each year during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check yearly what practical work I'd learned, what jobs it opened and whether the pay had improved. If the answers were empty, I'd change the route sooner. I wouldn't spend ten years being congratulated for courses that never reached a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans for the children now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't pick the children's studies from one card or put their future wages in our budget. I'd tell them adults still need teaching and can ask together for fair terms. I'd rather show them that than pretend I had every answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large wage loss before I've had time to test another skill. Paid practical training with covered fees and wages kept intact would help, as would someone checking what mortgage options really existed. My children need food while I'm learning, not a promise that learning will pay later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the saved hours. I can enjoy a new tool and still ask whether the people doing the work share the benefit. Being adaptable isn't consent to do the same job for less.

headlineQuote: My children need food while I'm learning, not a promise that learning will pay later.
portrait: **Beth, 43**, is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, ordinary trade skills and low pay among few nearby alternatives.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three weeks of normal expenses saved.
She uses AI **daily**, tests cheap tools early and favours collective requests that protect paid preparation and practical learning.
Fast change brings **alarm** over expected major wage loss; slower preparation eases learning pressure without erasing current money anxiety.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens a large wage loss before she can test another useful electrical skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** with covered fees and maintained wages would make learning possible.
Help checking actual **mortgage options** would clarify the household's choices without assuming approval.
